owner: W1-17. The layer every settlement's local answers hang off. RI-DLG01 §A: a topic exists ONCE, engine-wide; a hundred NPCs may have a hundred different answers to it.

infos.x: They are not unkind, the soldiers, they are only very tired and very wet, and a tired wet man will move you along off the boards without malice in a way that a rested dry one somehow never manages.

Nine hundred on paper. Four hundred standing. The rest is rot, fever, and the names on the muster board that draw the dead pay. We hold the cart roads and the two ferry crossings. Don't ask me about the interior.

The Ninth was raised for the Arnesian War and never stood down, which in Imperial practice means it was never funded again either. Its establishment is a document from the reign of a dead emperor and its actual strength is whatever the tribune can be persuaded to admit to in a given year.
Soldiers buy. The quartermaster does not pay. Friend, this one keeps two prices. Are you buying or asking?
Tribune Ancus Varo. Twelve years in post. He is not sent for and he sends for none, and the dead pay goes out under his hand every quarter. Draw your own conclusion, citizen.
The appointment of Ancus Varo is renewed by the silence of the Provincial Office. That is a valid mechanism under the establishment rules. It has run twelve years now without a signature on it.
The tribune. Old. Fair. Will not spend a man he cannot replace, and will not look too hard at the dead pay. Ask him yourself. He is in the wall house at Stormhold.
Were Varo a worse man he would be a richer one, and were he a better one he would have reported the dead pay years ago. He is precisely as honest as a man can be while remaining in post.

A muster board is a public document and it is never audited, which is the whole mechanism of the dead pay. On the Ninth's board there are names that have stood without interruption since before the fever year. A four-year posting is the usual term. Read it yourself. It is nailed up by the gate.
Names, ranks, watches, and the dead pay drawn against a few of them. Nailed by the gate. Read it and you know the garrison. Most people never read it.
You did not hear it from me. Twenty-one names on that board are dead. The pay still goes out. The paymaster signs for it and Ancus Varo signs after her. I am not asking who.

The discrepancy is arithmetical and therefore not deniable: the ration returns and the pay returns disagree by twenty-one men over four years, and rations are drawn by people who eat while pay is drawn by whoever the paymaster hands the chit to.
Quaestor Belena Sarn. Keeps the chest, keeps the ledger, keeps her own counsel. Why do you want the paymaster, citizen?
The pay woman buys nothing. Friend, buying nothing is not a thing people do, not when the dead pay passes through their hands. This one watches her.

Sarn came out to Stormhold with the last honest posting the Office made and has been here since, which is either a testament to her patience or evidence of something, the dead pay for instance, that she cannot afford to leave behind. The catalogue does not distinguish between those two states and neither, generally, does anyone else.
The Office. Yes. If you have a grievance, provincial, they will record it beautifully and file it against the charter. But they will not act on it, and I would not waste the morning.

The Office is the Empire's memory of Argonia, and it is a bad one. It surveys, it keeps the catalogue, it taxes, it issues the charter, and it does all of that on the assumption that the province is a version of Cyrodiil that has been rained on. The single most consequential document it holds is the Blackwater Treaty, which it has not opened in ninety years.
Clerks. They pay us late, every quarter, and never enough, and they have never once queried the dead pay. You'll want the annexe at Gideon. Go in the morning.
Paper. Presumably you've seen paper before. Whose charter are you asking about?

A charter is the Empire's way of saying that a thing which existed before it arrived now exists because of it. That is the imperial claim in a single sentence. Thorn has one, and it is genuine, and it is the only reason there is still a king in that hall.

Three years behind, and the years it is behind are the fever year and the two after it, which is exactly the period a person would want if they intended to look up who died and who inherited. The unfinished survey covers the same years. I mention this because I have been asked for those years four times this season, and by four people who did not know each other.

Everything off a boat goes on it. Weight, owner, port. Sign it or you lose it. If what you signed is the short weight, that is between you and the Ledger; if the cargo is contraband, that is between you and me. Have you got cargo coming in?
A manifest is a story about a cart, and the short weight is the best-loved chapter of it. And this one tells good stories, friend. Two drakes for a good one.
Hist sap weighs heavy wet. The Wet Ledger buys wet and sells dry. Friend, the difference is a cart in ten, and it isn't weighed twice. Don't say that in a Ledger room.

The practice is not fraud in the legal sense, because no weight is misstated; the fraud, if that is the word, is in the interval between the two weighings, and the interval is weather, and the weather is chosen by the wet ledger.
Contraband is only cargo with an opinion about it. Most of those opinions are formed on the cart roads. Friend, this one has opinions too.
Hist sap out of a well. Bone out of the xanmeers. Anything with a rootkeeper's mark. Carry it and you are ours, and the sanction is not a small one. Open the pack, citizen!

The Empire fines and the interior does not, and the reason is not mercy: a fine is a thing that ends, and the blood price owed to a family for a death is not a thing that ends, it is a thing that is carried until it is put down by agreement.
Fine first. Then the cell. Then Blackrose prison. Don't reach the third one, citizen, and pray it is never the blood price instead.

A death is owed to the kin, not to the province, and it is settled between them. No writ from any office in Cyrodiil extinguishes it. A ruling from an arbiter of ours does. The shadowscales are the other way it gets settled. So we do not say where the arbiters sleep.
Their law. Not ours. It still gets people killed, and it gets them killed fastest in the deep marshes. Watch yourself in the interior, citizen.

A ku-vastei hears what was done and says what is now true, and once it has been said the blood price is closed and the family that was owed will not pursue it, because to pursue it after a ruling is itself a debt. Where an arbiter cannot be reached, the shadowscales can.

They are given at the sign and raised apart and they do what is required, supplicant, and they are present at the naming of nobody. The covenant does not pretend it is clean; it says only that it is owed.

The Order is attested in Imperial records only as a category of exemption. It appears in a tax schedule annexed to the Blackwater Treaty, under persons not subject to inquiry, on the same page as the arbiters. The schedule has one entry and no name written against it.
Stories. Assassins under the boards. I have been here nine years. I have not seen one.
Wells make hist sap. Sap makes coin. Friend, this one is not permitted near them and the sap cutters are. This one buys from a man who is. Do you want the name or the price?

A well is a place where a root of the Great Hist has come near enough to the surface that the hist sap can be taken without cutting, and it is tended because a thing that gives without being cut is owed a great deal more than a thing that is harvested. That is the covenant in one sentence.

The Provincial Office classifies a sapwell as a mineral asset. A mineral asset is severable from the holding and may be licensed to a third party. The covenant has no view the Office is obliged to hear. Nine men have died on that clause since the survey.

It is not a medicine and it is not a drink. It is the Great Hist deciding something about you, supplicant, and the covenant is what you are deciding back. It is not always kind, and it is never quick, and it is never sold.

You are asking whether it can be shipped. House Dres has shipped it, at scale, for two centuries, and the organ market takes whatever they leave. The price reflects what happens to the people who ship it. Are you asking as a buyer or as an informant, provincial?
Small jar. Big price. The organ market pays double for it. Friend, this one doesn't ask what it does. Are you buying for yourself?

The one at Helstrom is the oldest that still speaks, and Helstrom is not a city that was built beside it but a city that was allowed inside it, and the difference is the whole of what we are. It is also the whole of the covenant, and it is why the quiet wells frighten us.
Every attested account agrees the tree predates the settlement at Helstrom. None agrees by how much. The estimates in the chronology range across a factor of nine. I have stopped citing any of them.

Fourteen wells have gone quiet in my lifetime, supplicant, and not one of them was cut; the dead well at Soulrest was the first of them. It is not the cutters, or not only the cutters. The covenant has no clause for it and the bad dreams began with it. I have said so at the well and been asked to say it again somewhere no one could hear.
Quiet well, no sap, no coin. Friend, this one has lost three of the cart roads this year. Have you been out east? Is the fourth still giving?

They say the wells are going quiet and they say it like it is weather, dry-one, but I slept by the dead well at Soulrest for six years and I can tell you it did not go quiet all at once, it went quiet the way a person does.

The keepers dream now. We did not before. The dreams come from the direction of the quiet wells, and the covenant says nothing whatever about dreaming. I have written this down four times and burned it three.

They are all having them on the boards and none will say so first, dry-one, and it is always the same one, and it is always a person standing in water that is warmer than water should be, and the ones who have worked near the quiet wells have it worst. I would not mind so much if I did not wake up glad.
Fever dreams, like the fever year come round again. Half the barracks has them. The physician says damp. So do I. Are you sleeping badly as well?

What is taken from the sapwells is returned, what is given at the naming is kept, and what is owed is carried; and where it is not carried, the blood price is. It is three sentences long and it has held for longer than the Empire has been able to write, and it is not a religion, supplicant, whatever the chapel tells you.

The Imperial position is that the covenant is a folk religion, and the provincial position among people who have actually lived here is that it is a body of property law with a tree at the top of it, and the second reading explains far more of the litigation, including most of the Blackwater Treaty.
This one has had four names, and two of them only work in Jel. Friend, you may use any of them. Which did you hear?

A hatchling is given a name at the well, in Jel, and it is a description, not a decoration, and it is expected to stop being true, at which point another is given and the first is not forgotten but is not used. The covenant asks only that somebody remember both.

The practice makes the census unusable. One man may appear three times in the catalogue under three descriptions and no clerk in Gideon can tell. The Office has also never sent anyone into the interior to count.

It is spoken where it is understood and it is not taught to those who would write it down, supplicant. It is the tongue of the naming and of nothing the Office keeps. The reason is not secrecy but that a written word cannot be taken back, and a great many of ours are meant to be.

Four Imperial attempts at a grammar survive and all four contradict each other on the tense system, and a fifth is bound into the unfinished survey and stops mid-paradigm. Either the language has no tense or it has one the surveyors could not hear. I incline to the second. All four had trouble with the word for river.

It is a paper about a promise that was not made in a language that has papers. It is the covenant with an Imperial seal on it, which is not the same thing. It has been kept anyway, supplicant, on both sides, for ninety years.
The treaty is why my estate is not an estate and why House Dres is here on sufferance. Should you find that funny, provincial, you would be in company.

Signed after the Arnesian War by an Argonian party the Empire has never fully identified and has never been able to say did not exist. It ended the raiding, it fixed the border, it exempted a category of person from imperial inquiry — the shadowscales, though it does not name them — and it contains the heirs clause, which has not been read since the year it was sealed.

Clause eleven. If a chartered holding has no heir the holding reverts, not to the Empire, but to the well that witnessed the charter, which in practice means one of the sapwells. Thorn is chartered and Thorn has no heir. Ninety years and no one has tested it. I intend to.

There is a clause in the treaty that has been transcribed wrongly in every subsequent copy. The original is in the Office annexe at Gideon, bound with the charter it qualifies. So far as I can make it out it reads as a reversion to a place rather than to a person. Imperial law has no procedure for that. I would like a second reader on the sheet before I write it down.
It is not a war in our telling, supplicant, it is a return, and the covenant is what was being returned to. The difference is that a war is fought against someone and a return is only walked.

A rebellion, provincial, against House Dres and against very little else. It was suppressed. Everything continued much as before, with a treaty laid on top of it. Did you want the Argonian telling? You will not get it from me.

Argonians rose against House Dres and against the slavers generally, and burned a good deal of the border and most of the slavers road with it, and were called savages for it in every account written by the people who had been holding them. The war is a hundred and eighty years old and the Ninth Cohort exists because of it and House Dres is still here because of it.
A road. If you are hoping I will apologise for a road on behalf of House Dres, provincial, you have misjudged the conversation. Was there something else?

The old road north still has the posts in it, dry-one, every forty paces the whole way to the border, and no one has pulled them up because pulling them up would be a thing an office had to decide. House Dres put them there. It has never once been counted among the cart roads.

They took from the wells and from the families for three hundred years and the Arnesian War settled none of it, and they are still here, and the covenant says what is owed is carried, so the blood price is carried.

Six estates, four factors, one magister and the Blackwater Treaty that says none of it is ours. The slavers road is closed and everyone knows what still moves along it. We remain because leaving would concede the point, as Magister Varo Dren never tires of explaining. Presumably that strikes you as absurd.
Dres pay well. Dres pay late. The organ market pays on the spot. And this one still goes, friend, twice a season.
Not our jurisdiction. Their estates, their law, and the sanction does not reach inside it. We do not go in.
I am he, if you were hoping for someone else. Were there a better magister available House Dres would have sent one thirty years ago. I have the heirs clause and a great deal of time.
The old Dunmer at the north estate, House Dres to the bone. Buys books. Pays in silver. Friend, this one knows no more than that. Have you a book?

The Ledger is a commercial house that happens to own the report chain: the manifest is written by their clerks and the factor at the far end of it is theirs as well. Owning the chain is more durable than owning the goods. In twenty years it has never once failed to know what a boat was carrying.
They lend, they buy, and the factor forgets a manifest. The short weight is theirs. So is half the organ market. Friend, they are not thieves. Thieves take once.
We know it is contraband. We cannot prove it is contraband. Every quarter the same.
Each town has one and the Wet Ledger owns them all. Quiet room, good chair, bad news. So ask for the quiet ledgerman, friend, not the factor. The factor won't see you.

He does not raise his voice and he does not need to, dry-one. He came up out of Soulrest and the Wet Ledger has never once had to send him a second letter. I have watched three men go into that room angry and come out arranging to pay for the privilege.
Not the Wet Ledger. Not near the organ market. Friend, don't put those two names in one sentence in a room. Who told you to ask me that?

They are the ones who were here before the Ledger and they have not agreed to stop being here, and if you want to know the difference, dry-one, the Ledger will ruin you and the Court will simply not have you found in the cut.

What is sold there is taken from wells and from bodies and from nests, supplicant, and every one of those is a thing the covenant says is returned. The Empire calls it contraband, and the market exists because the Empire's law has no word for the offence.
Hist sap, bone, egg, hide, and things this one does not name. Lilmoth, low tide, the drowned quarter under the second stair. Friend, don't go alone. Do you know anyone down there?

They call themselves cutters as though the cutting were the difficulty. The difficulty is that one of the sapwells which has been cut does not stop giving at once, and so the harm is not visible until the cutter is three towns away and cannot be shown it. That is how we came by the quiet wells.

A guild in the way a flock is a guild. This one pays dues, this one gets a route on the cart roads. So there is no hall and no master, friend, only Hard Bargain Jeel and a book. Do you want a route or a name?
Jeel runs the cart between three towns on the cart roads and buys anything the sap cutters bring down. Friend, don't sell to Jeel first. Sell to Jeel second. What have you got?
Known to us. No contraband proven. Yet.
The boards where there is water. Stone where the Empire could be bothered. And the drowned road where neither of them held, friend. The stone runs out at Gideon.
We patrol three. There are nine, and one of the nine is the drowned road, which we do not patrol at all. Where are you headed, citizen? I'll tell you if it's one of ours.

There was a proper Imperial road south of the Clay Moor and the marsh has had it back, dry-one, and nobody has laid the boards over it either. You can still walk it at the low tide of the year if you know where it goes under, and people do, and some of them come out the other side.

The southern trunk road is carried on the unfinished survey as extant. It is under four feet of water for most of the year. Correcting the sheet would require a man to go and look, and no man has been sent.

The boards are the province, dry-one, whatever the maps and the cart roads say, because everything that matters here happens on a plank two hands wide with water under it and a man coming the other way who will not give ground. Tide law says the water owns that plank twice a day, and it does.
Walk the boards, not the ground. Friend, this one's said it twice now. Are you listening?
Keep left. Give way to a laden man. It isn't courtesy, it is the sanction and the fine that comes with it. Two drakes, and I'd rather not write it out.
Everything is ownerless twice a day. That goes for the organ market too, friend, and this one owns a very good boat.
What the tide takes has no owner. What's above the line has one. Learn where the line runs, citizen, and ask again at every town. It moves, and the sanction moves with it.

The doctrine is Imperial in form and entirely native in substance: underneath it is the covenant, wearing a Cyrodiilic hat. Possession lapses at the high-water mark. In this province the high-water mark moves, and it moves a good deal, and no court has ever fixed it.

They were built when the wells were many and they are entered now only by the people who sell what is in them, supplicant, and every one of those people is carrying the blood price for it and has not been told.
There is one out past the ford in the eastern rootlands with the top off it and I would not sleep in it for any money, dry-one, and I have slept in a great many places you would not.

Solid, all the way through. The survey measured eleven of them with one rod and found no chamber in any, and what the guides sell as a chamber is a fall of the upper courses with a door cut into it by a guide's grandfather.

Step pyramids, pre-Imperial, and older than the settlements around them by an interval the chronology does not attempt; the ones standing in the stone forest are older still. They are not tombs, whatever the sale catalogues say; the interior arrangement is wrong for it, and the Office knows this and has never issued a correction, because the correction would depress the organ market it taxes.

There are three chronologies of this province in general use and they disagree by four hundred years at the Arnesian War, which is impossible, and the resolution is that one of them is counting from a different event and has never said which. The unfinished survey would have settled it. I have spent twenty years on that question and I am now reasonably confident that the event is a flood.

The survey of the eastern rootlands stops mid-sheet. The stated cause is weather. The surveyor's own note on the reverse says the party was ordered to withdraw by a man whose name has since been cut out of the paper with a knife, and the sheet is still in the annexe at Gideon, entered in the catalogue and asked for by nobody but me.
Surveyors went into the eastern rootlands. Came back short. Before my time. Why, what have you heard?

The wells were asked for more than they had and three of them stopped — the quiet wells, they are called now — and it has never been said aloud that the two things are one thing, supplicant, but it has been thought.

Four years back, dry-one. It took the boards first, because we're wet and thin. Then it went up the hill and took the ones with the dry beds. The physicians came and went and came back. And the bad dreams started that summer and never quite stopped. For one summer they carried our dead and we carried theirs.

The mortality is not recorded because the recording apparatus was itself among the mortality, which is a sentence I have written in a report and been asked to remove. The gap in the catalogue begins in that year and it is not a coincidence.

The chapel ones will see you if you're quiet and the Imperial ones will see you if you're paying, dry-one. But the bone-setter at Soulrest will see all comers, and she has nothing, and she has had nothing for years.
One per garrison. Overworked since the fever year and never replaced. Ours is good and ours drinks. Are you hurt, or asking for someone else?
They are here, supplicant, and they will not always be here, and what the covenant asks is only that we do not become them while we wait.

The claim rests on conquest that did not occur, cession that was never signed, and the Blackwater Treaty, which carefully does not use the word province. It is nonetheless entirely effective, because a claim is a thing that is administered rather than a thing that is true, and the Provincial Office administers it daily without ever having read it.

The name of the province is a lie of convenience: there is marsh, certainly — the deep marshes, and the eastern rootlands behind them — but there is also mountain at the Valus, the salt hills and arid rock in the west, the stone forest in the middle, the clay moor above it, jungle at Blackwood and a red littoral on the eastern coast. A traveller who expects swamp will spend a week being wrong in six different climates.
Thirteen names. Nine roads, and this one has walked every stretch of the cart roads worth walking. Friend, where are you bound?
Those were trees that did not agree to stop, supplicant, and they are not dead, they are only very slow, and the covenant does not permit them to be cut for exactly that reason.

Petrified growth standing where a living forest stood, and standing in the same arrangement, with the xanmeers among it. The Imperial explanation is gradual mineralisation. Gradual processes do not preserve a canopy. Helstrom and the Great Hist are inside it, not beside it.

I went up on the moor the summer of the fever year, dry-one, because a wet chest doesn't kill on the Clay Moor. Then I nearly died of thirst instead. They still tell it in Soulrest and they still laugh.
Dry uplands. Hard cart, and the best stretch of the cart roads, because the drowned road is what you get instead if you turn south. Friend, there's no water for a day. Carry it!

The unfinished survey stops here on every map I have handled, and the unfinished portions are not the same on any two of them. Either three surveys stopped at three different points, or one stopped and two draughtsmen guessed. The xanmeers are drawn in on one and absent from the others. I have asked the annexe for the field books twice.
We don't patrol east of the weeping ford. Orders, and old ones. No one asks why. And I'd rather you didn't either.

The interior is not empty and it is not lawless, supplicant; it is governed by the deep kin, who did not ask the Empire and will not, and by the covenant, which is older than the asking. A stranger who walks in without being brought in has made himself a question that will have to be answered.
Were the interior worth holding, provincial, it would have been held. It is not held. The Empire has never sent a cohort past the second ford and does not intend to.
In there we are a rumour and the deep kin are not. Go if you must. Go with a guide.

They kept what the coast put down, and they are not gentle about the difference. If you go into the deep marshes you will be measured against the covenant, which you have not read, and found short. Be quiet and you will come out again.
This one doesn't trade past the weeping ford. So don't ask, friend. This one likes this one's hands.
Dry. Hard. Ours. Stormhold sits on it. Best posting in the province, citizen — you sleep dry and your boots last a year.

Genuine jungle, canopy closed, and the only part of the province where Imperial agriculture has actually worked, which is why Gideon is there and why Gideon is insufferable. The Blackwood Company takes its name from it and does not operate in it.
Useful, if you are content to pay for enthusiasm rather than competence. House Dres retains them and House Dres does not discuss why.
Mercenaries. Paid better than us. Do less. Ask their recruiter at Gideon, not me.

They call it weeping for the sound the water makes on the stones. That is not true, dry-one, and everyone here knows it is not. It is called that because the slavers road crossed here, and it has been agreed to forget.
A crossing on the Helstrom leg of the cart roads, and the last of them before the eastern rootlands. Deep at the turn. Friend, wait for the boards to show.

The channel behind the warehouses at Lilmoth, dry-one, and things come out of it that went in somewhere else entirely. The Cohort fishes them out and writes drowned and everyone is satisfied except the ones who watched. Ask about the man in the water. Then ask why the drowned court has never read for a single one of them.
Bad water. Worst district in Lilmoth. Four this year, all drowned. Do you know one of them?

He walked down into the cut on his own feet with a man behind him not hurrying. That is not a drowning, however it is written up, and the drowned court has not read for him. I've told three people. Two told me to be quieter. The third was the ledgerman of Lilmoth, and he asked me where I sleep.
One of the four out of the cut. Nothing on him. The case is closed, citizen. Who's been talking to you?
The man the Wet Ledger keeps at Lilmoth. Never leaves the room. Friend, everything in that quarter goes past his chair, and so does everything that goes into the cut.

It is a day east of the weeping ford, in the eastern rootlands, and it is on no roll, and it is not among the quiet wells. The keeper who found it kept it off the rolls herself, and I have never decided whether she was protecting it from the cutters or from us.
Arms, boots, oil, for the Ninth Cohort and nobody else. Requisition only. No, not for you, not without a chit. And do not ask him about the dead pay. Have you got one? Then move along!
Two drakes on the book. Five in the hand. The difference is what makes a cargo contraband. Friend, this one pays the two.
Two drakes on a cart. Nothing on a person. Anyone charging you more is stealing, and the sanction is the same for him as it would be for you. Who took more off you?
The roll of the tithed, kept at the Chapel of Akatosh. In Gideon that is very nearly the roll of the respectable. Two names on it will surprise you. Ask the priest, not me.

The priest at Gideon is not a fool and is not a traitor to his order, supplicant; he has simply understood that a well and an altar are asked for by the same people at the same hours for the same reasons, and that the covenant does not much mind who is holding the cup.

A proper chapel at Gideon, stone, with a bell that was carried here in pieces, the tithe roll kept in a fair hand, and a priest who has been quietly conducting the rites of the covenant in the vestry for a dozen years on the entirely reasonable grounds that the people asking for them are his parish.
It's called a forest and it's a field of spikes as tall as a hall, dry-one. There's one path through it. All of Thorn knows it and no map has it. Are you going that way? Take someone with you.
Thornwood, cut at Thorn. Straight grain. House Dres buys it for bows. Friend, the Empire buys it for spears.

The vats at Archon take a season off your hands and ten years off your lungs, dry-one. The yard pays a wage that is very slightly better than the alternative. There's a queue at the gate every morning.
Tide-lichen off the crimson coast, boiled at Archon. Comes out imperial purple. Friend, the Empire pays for the colour of its own gowns.

The colour is lichen and the lichen is seasonal, so the coast south of Archon is red for four months and grey for eight, and every Imperial painting of it was made in the four. The Provincial Office and its revenue projections were also made in the four.

It stopped in my mother's time and Soulrest has stayed, supplicant. That is not stubbornness. A well that has stopped is still owed the tending under the covenant, and the tending falls to them, as it does at all the quiet wells.
They still walk down to it at the tide-turn, dry-one, the whole of Soulrest, and stand there, and go home, and they have not been told to stop and none would dare.
Half of Blackrose has kin in it and the other half works in it, dry-one. At the end of a shift they drink together. I've never got used to it.
Imperial. Long sentences. Full. It is the last step of the sanction and it stands at Blackrose. Do not end up in it, citizen.

The prison at Blackrose is the largest Imperial structure in the province, and its population is recorded in the catalogue to the individual, name by name. Every other population figure the Office holds for Argonia is an estimate.
Old Imperial stone under Lilmoth. Sunk to the first windows. The organ market is down there and so is the cut. Friend, people still live in the second.

Two cities occupying the same plan at different elevations, the lower one Imperial and submerged, the upper one native and built on top of it. Lilmoth is the imperial claim in cross-section. You can row down the old main street at high water and read the shop signs.
